title: The Sun bends starlight
teaches: How gravity slows time, why that makes things fall and bends light, and how Mercury, an eclipse and the satellites in your phone test it

blocks.text: *A planet found with a pen* ended with a planet that wasn't there. Mercury's stretched orbit slowly turns, and after every other planet's pull is added up by Newton's law, a little turning is left over: 43 seconds of arc a century (a second of arc is a 3,600th of a degree), about the width of a coin seen from a hundred metres. Le Verrier, who had found Neptune by trusting the law and adding an unseen planet, tried the same trick and invented Vulcan. Eclipse expeditions hunted for it near the darkened Sun for fifty years. It wasn't there.

So the other answer, the one nobody wanted, must be right: Newton's law of gravity, the most successful law in science, was slightly wrong. Nobody could see how to fix it. A law that works to one part in ten million everywhere else isn't easy to adjust in one place without breaking it in all the others. The fix, when it came, didn't adjust the law. It replaced the idea of what gravity is, and it grew out of a thought Einstein had at his desk in the patent office in 1907.

“If a person falls freely,” Einstein realised, “he will not feel his own weight.” He later called it the happiest thought of his life. You met it in *The falling Moon*: astronauts float in the space station not because there is no gravity up there, but because they and the station are falling round the Earth together. Inside a falling box there is no way to tell that you are in gravity at all. Drop an apple and it hangs beside you.

Einstein took that seriously. If falling cancels gravity completely, then everything that happens inside a falling box must happen as if there were no gravity. Shine a torch across the box and the light goes straight across. But the box is falling, so seen from outside, the light must have curved downwards with it. Gravity bends light.

Now shine the torch upward, from the floor of a room on the ground to the ceiling. The light is climbing against gravity, and Einstein's same reasoning says it arrives with a little less energy: slightly redder, its waves slightly further apart, as if it had been sent from a clock ticking slower. That is exactly what it means. A clock on the floor runs slow compared with one on the ceiling. Lower down, time itself goes slightly slower.

The difference is absurdly small: over the height of a house, a few parts in a million billion. In 1959 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka at Harvard measured it anyway. They sent gamma rays, a very energetic kind of light, 22.5 metres up a tower in the physics building, and down again, and found them shifted by just the amount Einstein's argument said, to within ten percent. Later experiments got it to within a few parts in a hundred thousand, and today's best atomic clocks can see the difference when one is lifted a few centimetres.

parts.title: The path the clock likes best

blocks.text: You have probably seen gravity drawn as a heavy ball on a rubber sheet, with marbles rolling round the dent. It is a lovely picture and it explains nothing: the marbles roll into the dent because gravity pulls them down, which uses gravity to explain gravity. Worse, it leaves out time, and for anything moving slowly, time is almost the whole story.

Here is what Einstein's gravity says about a thrown ball, in its simplest form. Carry a watch with it. Two things change how fast the watch ticks. Higher up, time runs faster, so the watch gains by climbing. Moving, the watch runs slow (that was *Muons that live too long*), so it loses by going fast. Of all the paths that leave your hand and reach your friend's two seconds later, the one the ball actually takes is the one on which its watch ticks the most.

blocks.caption: A ball thrown up and caught two seconds later, and how many extra ticks a watch riding on it collects, compared with one left on the ground. The circles mark the watch along the way.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then find the path on which the watch ticks the most

blocks.text: Go too low and the watch misses out on the faster time higher up. Go too high and, to be back in two seconds, it must race up and down so fast that its speed costs more than its height gains. The best trade is exactly the arc Newton would have calculated. The ball doesn't need a force telling it where to go. Things fall because time runs at different rates at different heights, and a falling body follows the path its own clock likes best. The numbers are tiny (the winning watch beats the one on the ground by a third of a millionth of a billionth of a second), but that tiny difference is the whole of the Earth's pull on the ball.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Clocks lower down run slower. For slow-moving things, that difference in time is what gravity is.
A thrown ball, a falling apple and an orbiting Moon each follow the path on which a clock carried with them would tick the most.

parts.title: Half the answer, then the whole

blocks.text: In 1911 Einstein worked out how much the Sun should bend the light of a star just grazing its edge: a little under one second of arc, the same as you get by treating light as a Newtonian bullet. The only time stars can be seen next to the Sun is in a total eclipse, so he asked astronomers to photograph one. In August 1914 a German expedition led by Erwin Freundlich set off for an eclipse in the Crimea. Germany declared war on Russia while they were on the way. They were arrested as spies, their instruments were confiscated, and the eclipse came and went.

It was a lucky failure. Einstein's 1911 number was wrong. Over the next four years he struggled to turn his falling-box idea into a full theory, in which matter tells space and time how to curve and the curving tells matter how to move. In November 1915 he finished it, and two things fell out at once. Light grazing the Sun should bend twice as much as he'd said, about 1.75 seconds of arc, because space near the Sun is stretched as well as time. And Mercury's orbit should turn by exactly 43 seconds of arc a century more than Newton allowed. Einstein said his heart fluttered when he saw the number come out. He had not been trying to fit it.

This is **general relativity**: general, because it covers gravity and every kind of motion, not just the steady motion of special relativity. Mercury's riddle was solved not by an unseen mass but by a new law, and Vulcan could finally be forgotten.

The war was barely over when the British astronomer Arthur Eddington sailed to Príncipe, an island off West Africa, and a second team went to Sobral in Brazil, to photograph the eclipse of 29 May 1919. The Sun would be passing in front of a bright cluster of stars, the Hyades, which was a piece of luck. Eddington, a Quaker who had refused to fight, was keen to show that science could cross the lines of a war, and that an English expedition could confirm a German's theory.

blocks.caption: Stars beside the eclipsed Sun are seen pushed outwards, away from it, compared with where the same stars are at night. Stars nearer the Sun's edge are pushed more.

blocks.text: Clouds covered Príncipe until the last moments; Eddington got a few usable plates. The Sobral team had clear skies but trouble with heat warping one of their telescopes. The results were rough: one set of plates gave about 1.6 seconds of arc, another about 2.0, and a third, from the warped telescope, gave nearly Newton's half value and was set aside. In November the results were announced in London: Einstein was right. “Revolution in Science,” said *The Times*, and Einstein was famous overnight.

Was Eddington fair? Historians have argued about it ever since. The measurements were near the limit of what the plates could show, and leaving out the awkward set looks suspicious. But there were real reasons to distrust it, and when the Sobral plates were measured again in 1979 with modern machines, even the rejected ones came out on Einstein's side. Since the 1970s, radio telescopes timing quasars as the Sun passes near them have confirmed the bending to better than one part in a thousand. Eddington's answer was right, even if his evidence was thinner than the headlines.

A big enough mass bends light enough to act as a lens. When a far galaxy lies exactly behind a nearer one, the nearer galaxy's pull bends its light round both sides, and we see the far galaxy smeared into a ring. This is **gravitational lensing**, and the rings are called Einstein rings. Astronomers now use lensing to weigh galaxies and clusters, which turns out to matter a great deal in *Unseen mass or a wrong law?*

blocks.caption: How a near galaxy bends a far galaxy's light into a ring.

blocks.text: If this all sounds remote, check your phone's map. GPS works by timing radio signals from satellites 20,200 kilometres up, each carrying an atomic clock. Your phone works out how far away each satellite is from how long its signal took, at the speed of light, and a billionth of a second of error is thirty centimetres.

blocks.caption: A clock in orbit against a clock on the ground: what it gains in a day from being higher, and loses from moving fast.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then put a clock where a GPS satellite is

blocks.text: Both kinds of relativity are at work. Up there, gravity is weaker, so the satellites' clocks run faster, by about 46 millionths of a second a day. They also move at nearly 4 kilometres a second, so special relativity slows them by about 7. Together they gain about 38 millionths of a second a day, and light covers about 11 kilometres in that time. Without the correction, your position would drift by kilometres every day. The engineers set the satellites' clocks to tick very slightly slow before launch, so that in orbit they keep time with the ground. Every time you find your way with a phone, you are using Einstein's theory of gravity.

blocks.caption: Six questions on gravity, time and light
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Two identical clocks, one on the ground floor and one at the top of a tall tower. After a year, which shows more time passed?
choices: The one on the ground floor
items.why: Higher up, time runs faster. Pound and Rebka saw the difference over 22.5 metres; GPS satellites gain 46 millionths of a second a day from it.

items.ask: Why does the rubber-sheet picture of gravity explain nothing?
choices: The marbles roll into the dent because of gravity, and it leaves out time
It uses the wrong mass for the Sun
Space is not curved at all
items.why: It needs gravity to pull the marbles down the slope. For slow-moving things, gravity is almost all about time running at different rates at different heights.

items.ask: Seen from inside a falling lift, a beam of light goes straight across. Seen from outside, it…
items.why: The lift falls while the light crosses it, so from outside the light's path bends down with it. That was Einstein's first argument that gravity bends light.

items.ask: How did Mercury's orbit get explained in the end?
choices: A new law of gravity, general relativity, gives exactly the extra 43 seconds of arc a century
The Sun turned out to be heavier
items.why: No unseen planet: this time the law was wrong. Einstein's theory gave the 43 seconds without being adjusted to fit them.

items.ask: GPS satellite clocks gain about 46 millionths of a second a day from height and lose about 7 from speed. A satellite in a much lower orbit moves faster. What happens to its clock?
choices: It gains less, or even loses, compared with the ground
items.why: Lower down it gains less from height and loses more from speed. Clocks on the space station, 400 km up, actually run slow compared with the ground.

items.ask: Why did astronomers in 1919 have to wait for a total eclipse?
choices: Only then can stars be seen close to the Sun
The Moon bends the light too
The Sun bends light only during an eclipse
items.why: The bending is biggest for light grazing the Sun's edge, and only in an eclipse is the sky dark enough to photograph stars there.

summary: **Mercury's orbit turns too fast.** 43 seconds of arc a century more than Newton's law allows, and Vulcan was never found.
**Falling cancels weight.** Einstein's happiest thought: inside a falling box there is no gravity, so light seen from outside must bend.
**Lower clocks run slower.** Pound and Rebka measured it up a 22.5-metre tower in 1959.
**Gravity is time running at different rates.** A thrown ball follows the path on which a watch carried with it ticks the most.
**General relativity, 1915.** It gave Mercury's 43 seconds and twice the bending of starlight Einstein had first predicted.
**The 1919 eclipse.** Stars beside the Sun were seen shifted, roughly as predicted; later radio measurements settled it.
**Gravitational lensing.** A galaxy can bend a farther galaxy's light into an Einstein ring.
**GPS needs both relativities.** Satellite clocks gain about 38 millionths of a second a day, about 11 km of error if uncorrected.
